questions.q: What problem does an Airflow Connection solve?
options: Python import errors in DAG files
Tasks not retrying on failure
Credentials and connection details getting hardcoded and copy-pasted across every DAG that needs them
DAGs running too slowly
questions.explain: A Connection stores credentials/connection details exactly once, under an ID, instead of repeating them in every DAG.

options: The name of the Airflow scheduler process
The short name a DAG uses to reference a stored Connection, without holding its secret
The password itself, stored in plain text in the DAG file
A unique ID assigned to every task instance
questions.explain: conn_id is the link between a DAG and a Connection record — the DAG never touches the actual credential.

questions.q: Where in the Airflow UI do you view and add Connections?
options: Browse > Task Instances
Admin > Connections
Home > Dashboard
Docs > API Reference
questions.explain: Connections are managed under the Admin section of the Airflow UI.

questions.q: What does the "Extra" field on a Connection hold?
options: A JSON blob for settings specific to that connection type, not covered by the standard fields
A list of every task that uses the connection
The DAG's schedule interval
A backup copy of the password
questions.explain: Extra is a flexible JSON field — for example, a Snowflake connection might use it to store the account, warehouse, and role.

questions.q: In `SnowflakeOperator(task_id="run_query", snowflake_conn_id="snowflake_default", sql="...")`, what does the DAG file itself actually know about the Snowflake password?
options: Nothing — the password lives only in the Connection record and is resolved at run time
The full password, written directly in the code
The password is passed as a command-line argument
Only the first few characters, for validation
questions.explain: The DAG only references the conn_id; the actual credential resolution happens when the task runs, not in the DAG's source code.
